newsitem.title: USA: Chicago economists see 1997 inflation staying low.
newsitem.headline: Chicago economists see 1997 inflation staying low.

text.p: Economists at the University of Chicago's annual business outlook press conference Wednesday said they saw inflation in check in 1997, but they differed on the strength of the U.S. economy.

John Huizinga, a University of Chicago professor of business economics, predicted the U.S. economy would grow more slowly next year at 2.1 percent, with overall inflation rising slightly to 2.2 percent.
Huizinga said 1996 would likely finish with 2.3 percent growth and overall inflation of 2.1 percent.

Energy prices are the primary concern for the 1997 economy, he said. Skyrocketing energy prices in 1996 have pushed the fuel component of producer prices up more than 14 percent in the last year, he said.
"Increases of this magnitude have, in the past, led to a slowdown of economic activity," he said.

Huizinga said expectations for "bland growth" and a recently enacted hike in the minimum wage would lift the unemployment rate by 0.2 percentage point in 1997. The U.S. jobless rate is currently 5.2 percent.

Joel Stern, managing partner with Stern Stewart & Company, had a more bullish outlook for the economy, predicting 3.0 percent real growth next year and 30-year government bond yields testing six percent. The long bond was yielding 6.37 percent in trading on Wednesday.
He pegged the consumer price index in 1997 up 2.3 percent, the GDP price deflator up 1.8 percent and producer prices up 1.2 percent.
"However, growth will not be large enough to warrant a resurgence in inflationary expectations, nor will the average rate of unemployment change from where it is now," Stern said.
On the global front, University of Chicago professor Marvin Zonis said he expects "a year precisely made for the continued success and globalization of American businesses."
Zonis cited general price stability, growing world trade, and the spread of market economies and political democracy.
